sentences.text: Most known fossils of this dinosaur consist of the front part of the animal.
Preservation evidence suggests the head and neck armor may have detached from the body before burial.
Ziapelta sanjuanensis possesses three unique derived traits that distinguish it from other dinosaurs.
A large, prominent, triangular bone plate sits in the middle of its snout.
The widest part of the skull is formed by the squamosal horns at the top rear corners, with no constriction in front of the eyes.
The upper jaws measured 11.9 centimeters in length and held approximately eighteen small teeth on each side.
The body was protected by osteoderms, which are bone scutes embedded in the skin.
Individuals of this genus measured between 4.6 and 6.1 meters in length.
The skull had a length of about 44 centimeters.
The genus Ziapelta was named in 2014 by a research team led by Victoria Arbour.
Fossils were discovered in 2011 by an expedition led by Robert Michael Sullivan.
There is only one known species in the genus, named Ziapelta sanjuanensis.
The genus name combines the Zia sun symbol and the Latin word 'pelta', referencing the animal's armor.
The species name 'sanjuanensis' refers to San Juan County, the location of the fossil discovery.
A 2011 expedition led by Robert Michael Sullivan discovered the fossils in the Kirtland Formation.
The specimens were found in the Hunter Wash and De-na-zin members of the formation within the Bisti/De-Na-Zin Reserve in New Mexico.
The holotype specimen NMMNH P-64484 consists of a complete skull lacking jaws, parts of the first two cervical rings, and a series of partial osteoderms.
Ziapelta is classified in the family Ankylosauridae and is considered a sister species to Scolosaurus from Canada in several evolutionary trees.
An alternative hypothesis suggests Ziapelta and Nodocephalosaurus could be sister species, though this requires only one additional shared trait and is slightly less likely.
The closest relative of Ziapelta is debated, with Scolosaurus or Nodocephalosaurus proposed depending on the cladistic model used.
Researchers propose that ankylosaurids recolonized North America from Asia during the Campanian or Turonian ages, leading to the diversification of genera including Ziapelta.
The absence of Ziapelta in habitats shared by relatives like Euoplocephalus and Scolosaurus does not prove faunal separation, as Ziapelta comes from younger geological layers.
Ziapelta is classified as an extinct genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur.
Ziapelta belongs to the family Ankylosauridae.
Ziapelta is classified within the class Ornithischia.
Ziapelta and other Late Cretaceous North American ankylosaurs are grouped with Asian genera in a tribe named Ankylosaurini.
The parent group of Ziapelta is the tribe Ankylosaurini.
The species Ziapelta sanjuanensis was described by Arbour, Burns, Sullivan, Lucas, and Cantrell in 2014.
Ziapelta lived during the Upper Cretaceous (Campanian) period in New Mexico.
Ziapelta lived in North America between 74.5 and 72.5 million years ago during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
Argon dating of ash layers determined the holotype skull's age to be between 72.98 and 72.62 million years old, during the late Campanian.
The genus Ziapelta lived from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago during the Campanian stage.
